summary:
Adygea stands under the framework of Russia, where same-sex marriage and legal gender transition are prohibited, trans-specific healthcare has been effectively banned since 2023, and no anti-discrimination protection is in force. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) sets out this national framework and records that 139 people were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws across Russia between 2022 and 2024.

The same note assesses that lesbian, gay and bisexual people in Russia are not generally at real risk of persecution solely for their sexual orientation, while people in the North Caucasus, trans people, and those publicly active in LGBT+ advocacy are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. Adygea, as a North Caucasus republic, is not named as an exception to that assessment; a trans visitor or publicly active advocate is therefore assessed as facing a real risk of persecution here.

Extremism charges following the designation of the 'International LGBT Movement' are documented at scale. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 'extremism'-related convictions by 30 June 2025 for alleged participation in that movement or display of its symbols, comprising 98 administrative and 3 criminal convictions. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges: two were sentenced to prison and seventeen cases remain pending or of unknown outcome.

Penalties under the extremism provisions are severe. On 15 May 2025, three staff of two publishing houses were charged with 'running an extremist organization' under article 282.2 and face up to 12 years in prison. Repeated display of banned symbols is punishable with up to four years in prison.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia covers the North Caucasus republics, which includes Adygea, and imposes interior-permission entry regimes requiring authorisation to travel within the region.
tangentialFactors:
The North Caucasus carries a distinct risk profile within Russia: the UK Home Office note singles out people in this region, alongside trans people and public LGBT+ advocates, as likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, in contrast to its assessment for LGB people nationally. Adygea sits within that singled-out category.

The US State Department advisory's interior-permission regime for the North Caucasus republics means movement into and within Adygea is subject to additional permits beyond standard Russian entry requirements, adding a documentation checkpoint at which identity documents may be examined.
localsOnly:
Trans residents of Adygea cannot obtain legal gender recognition, access trans-specific healthcare (banned since 2023), or benefit from any anti-discrimination protection on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation. The UK Home Office assessment treats trans people in Russia, and people in the North Caucasus specifically, as likely to face persecution, indicating a materially worse position for local trans residents than for LGB residents in most of Russia.

The 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws across Russia between 2022 and 2024, recorded in the June 2025 UK Home Office note, provide a national figure; no Adygea-specific breakdown of that count is given in the sources.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not document Adygea-specific enforcement incidents, local court outcomes, or regional administrative practice under the extremism or propaganda provisions; the extremism conviction figures are national totals for Russia and are not disaggregated by republic.

No Adygea-specific figure is available for how many of the 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws between 2022 and 2024 were located in this republic, and the sources do not resolve whether interior-permission checks in Adygea have been used to screen or flag gender-nonconforming travellers.
